content: Kvass, a term derived from the Russian word квас meaning leaven, is a mildly alcoholic beverage produced through the fermentation of black or rye bread. It has been a popular drink in Russia, Belarus, Ukraine, and other Eastern and Central European countries, as well as in former Soviet states like Uzbekistan, where street vendors commonly sell it. Due to its low alcohol content (typically less than 1.2%), it is considered safe for children to consume. Kvass is often enhanced with flavors from fruits or herbs, such as strawberries or mint. In Russian cuisine, it is also used as a base for a traditional cold summer soup called okroshka. Kvass has a long history in Eastern Europe, dating back to ancient times. It was first mentioned in Old Russian chronicles in the year 989. Historically, it has been both a commercially produced and homemade beverage. It was widely consumed across Slavic countries, and street vendors selling kvass were a common sight in many cities. The production of kvass involves the natural fermentation of bread made from wheat, rye, or barley. It is sometimes flavored with fruits, berries, raisins, or birch sap collected in early spring. The fermentation process typically includes the use of a yeast culture and a starter known as zakvasska. Commercially produced kvass is often made similarly to other soft drinks, using sugar, carbonated water, malt extract, and flavorings. Kvass is usually served unfiltered, retaining the yeast, which contributes to its distinctive flavor and high vitamin B content. Kvass is known by different names in various languages. In Russian, Belarusian, Serbian, and Ukrainian, it is called квас (kvass). In Polish, it is referred to as kwas chlebowy, which translates to bread leaven. In Lithuanian, it is called gira, and in Estonian, it is known as kali. In Latvia, the sale of kvass underwent significant changes after the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991. New health regulations banned street sales of kvass, and economic disruptions led to the closure of many kvass factories. During this time, the Coca-Cola company entered the market and quickly dominated the soft drink industry. However, in 1998, the local soft drink industry launched a counter-effort by selling bottled kvass and implementing aggressive marketing campaigns. This resurgence was further fueled by the fact that kvass was sold at about half the price of Coca-Cola. Within three years, kvass accounted for up to 30% of the soft drink market in Latvia, while Coca-Cola's market share dropped from 65% to 44%. Coca-Cola experienced losses of approximately $1 million in Latvia during 1999 and 2000. Similar trends were observed in other Baltic countries and in Russia. In response, Coca-Cola began acquiring kvass manufacturers and started producing kvass in their soft drink plants.
